title: You built a Roman apartment block

lines.text: Your city is packed with people, and there's no land left to build on.
So you build up, starting with a ground floor of brick-faced concrete.
You open every front room onto the street and rent it to a baker or a cobbler. This is a taberna.
But a row of shops won't house all the workers pouring into the city.
So you stack apartments on top, with thick brick walls on the lower floors.
The wealthiest tenants take the lower floors, steadier and closest to the street.
But brick and concrete are expensive, and you want more floors, fast.
So the upper floors go up in cheap timber and mudbrick.
Up here there is no kitchen and no plumbing. Tenants haul water from the public fountain and buy dinner from street stalls.
The higher you climb, the smaller and cheaper the rooms, until the poorest families are crammed under the roof. This is an insula.
But one Roman poet complained that most buildings were held up by flimsy bits of wood.
Even Cicero admitted some of his rental buildings were falling down.
And timber burns. In the Great Fire of sixty four, flames swept through entire districts of these blocks.
So the law steps in. No new building may rise higher than seventy Roman feet, about twenty one meters.
Later, Emperor Trajan cuts the limit again, to sixty feet.
Even so, ancient lists count over forty thousand of these blocks in Rome, and fewer than two thousand private houses.
Congratulations. You have built an insula.
